inline.s: Or there may be a bhikṣu who, having left home and received the precepts because of my Dharma, strives diligently within this Dharma; even though the gods and men do not come to make offerings, if he can single-mindedly and diligently practice the way, in the end he will not lack the clothing and food he needs. Why is this? Because the Tathāgata’s store of merit is immeasurable and inexhaustible. Śāriputra, after the Tathāgata’s passing, of the hundred thousand crore portions of the mark of the white hair, one portion is given to support the relics and the disciples. Śāriputra, were all the people of the world to leave home and follow the true Dharma in practice, they would not exhaust one of the hundred thousand crore portions of the white-hair mark. Śāriputra, such is the Tathāgata’s immeasurable merit that the food and the things those bhikṣus obtain are all fully provided. Śāriputra, these bhikṣus should think in this way, and should not, for the sake of the things they need, take up any wrong means of livelihood.
[Wrong means of livelihood]Taking up unwholesome occupations in order to sustain one’s life.

[Śāriputra, a bhikṣu who wears the patched robe and has gathered old castoffs from the dust-heaps should think thus: “I wear this in order to ward off cold and to cultivate the noble path; with these castoffs I now sew a samghāṭi and wear it, striving diligently in practice.” If his mind is that of a common person, he should not wear it even for a single night. Such a bhikṣu should wash it clean, sew it, and wear it. If this bhikṣu, in this patched robe, gives rise to thoughts of grasping and attachment, he should at once give it up — I do not permit him to wear it, much less other robes. Why? Śāriputra, because this bhikṣu, in this robe, gives rise to what is not the Dharma of a bhikṣu. Such a bhikṣu should no longer wear it, much less any other object! Śāriputra, at that time a bhikṣu would rather wrap his body in red-hot iron plates (thin iron sheets) than wear this patched robe. Why? Because of the mind of attachment produced toward this robe. Śāriputra, a bhikṣu of the patched robe should think thus: “I wear this patched robe to ward off cold and heat and to assist the path; now I will wear no other robe and shall attain the fruit of stream-enterer, once-returner, non-returner, and arhat.” Śāriputra, to a bhikṣu of the patched robe who single-mindedly seeks the way, I give permission to wear it.]

Śāriputra, when a bhikṣu has gathered old and worn-out clothing or rags from among the dust, washed them clean, made of them a patched robe, and put it on, he should think thus: “I wear this to ward off cold and to cultivate the noble path; I should strive diligently in practice.” If his mind is that of a common person, he should not wear it even for a single night. If this bhikṣu gives rise to thoughts of grasping and attachment toward this patched robe, he should take it off (because attachment is a common-person’s mind) — I do not permit him to wear it, much less other robes. Why? Śāriputra, because this bhikṣu, in this robe, gives rise to what is not the Dharma of a bhikṣu (he gives rise to thoughts contrary to the Dharma). Such a bhikṣu should no longer wear this patched robe, much less any other object! Śāriputra, at that time a bhikṣu would rather wrap his body in red-hot thin iron sheets than wear this patched robe. Why? Because of the mind of attachment produced toward this robe. Śāriputra, a bhikṣu of the patched robe should think thus: “I wear this patched robe to ward off cold and heat and to assist the path; now I will wear no other robe and shall attain the fruit of stream-enterer, once-returner, non-returner, and arhat.” Śāriputra, to such a bhikṣu of the patched robe who single-mindedly seeks the way, I give permission to wear it.

[Patched robe]Also called the dust-heap robe: the old, worn-out clothing or rags discarded among the dust, gathered up, washed clean, and sewn into a Dharma robe. [Samghāṭi]Here it refers to the patched robe. [Common person]An ordinary being deluded about the principles of things and wandering in birth-and-death. [Iron plates (

[Śāriputra, a bhikṣu who lives by begging alms should make no discriminations among dharmas; he should constantly gather his mind and not let it scatter when he enters the village, adorning himself with the various concentrations. Having obtained his alms, with a mind unstained, he takes the food he has received and leaves the village. At a spot by clean water suitable for practice, he sets the food aside, washes his feet, and sits down. Placing the food before him, he should give rise to the perception of revulsion, the perception of impurity, the perception of excrement and urine, the perception of rottenness, the perception of being vomited, the perception of a smeared sore, the perception of disgust, the perception of a child’s flesh, the perception of a foul fruit, the perception of heaviness; and within the body he should give rise to the perception of death, the perception of blueness, the perception of matter, the perception of decay.]

Śāriputra, a bhikṣu who lives by begging alms should make no discriminations among dharmas; he should constantly gather his mind and not let it scatter when he enters the village, adorning himself with the various concentrations. Having finished begging, with a mind unstained, he takes the food he has received and leaves the village. At a spot by clean water suitable for practice, he sets the food aside, washes his feet, and sits down. Before eating, he should give rise toward the food to the perception of revulsion, the perception of impurity, the perception of excrement and urine, the perception of rottenness, the perception of being vomited, the perception of a smeared sore, the perception of disgust, the perception of a child’s flesh, the perception of a foul fruit, the perception of heaviness; and within the body he should give rise to the perception of death, the perception of blueness, the perception of matter, the perception of decay.
[Village]A settlement, a village; that is, a place where the multitudes dwell together.

[Śāriputra, a bhikṣu should give rise to this thought and then eat with a mind free of attachment, merely to sustain the body, to dispel hunger, thirst, and illness, and so to be able to cultivate the path. He should think: “I eat this food to break through earlier suffering and not to give rise to later suffering; my mind attains joy, is attuned and without affliction, my body is light, and my steps are at ease.” And again he should think: “Having eaten this food, I should attain the fruit of stream-enterer, once-returner, non-returner, and arhat, and the patience of non-production.” Śāriputra, a bhikṣu who eats in this way — I permit him to beg for alms. Śāriputra, if a bhikṣu who begs for alms, toward the food he has obtained, gives rise to a mind greedily savoring it and thinks it delicious, and thinks: “Eating this food I shall gain a good complexion and abundant strength,” and does not think: “Eating this food I strive along the noble path” — such a bhikṣu I do not permit to receive so much as a single cup of water, much less food.]

Śāriputra, this bhikṣu should give rise to this thought and then eat with a mind free of attachment, merely to sustain the body, to dispel hunger, thirst, and illness, and so to be able to cultivate the path. He should think: “I eat this food to break through earlier suffering and not to give rise to later suffering; my mind attains joy, is attuned and without affliction, my body is light, and my steps are at ease.” And again he should think: “Having eaten this food, I should attain the fruit of stream-enterer, once-returner, non-returner, and arhat, and the patience of non-production.” Śāriputra, a bhikṣu who eats in this way — I permit him to beg for alms. Śāriputra, if a bhikṣu who begs for alms, toward the food he has obtained, gives rise to a mind greedily savoring it and thinks it delicious, and thinks: “Eating this food I shall gain a good complexion and abundant strength,” and does not think: “Eating this food I strive along the noble path” — such a bhikṣu I do not permit to receive so much as a single cup of water, much less food.
[Patience of non-production]That is, the patience of non-arising.

[Śāriputra, if one eats without seeing the evil in food and without seeing the way out, it were better that he cut flesh from his own thigh with his own hand and eat it. Why? Because I permit practitioners and attainerers to receive the offerings of others; I do not permit the rest. Śāriputra, what is called a practitioner? If there is a bhikṣu who has firmly resolved, “In this very life I will cut off the fetters and the driving defilements and enter the nirvāṇa of no remainder; I cultivate the noble path as though my head were afire, and I will also cut off and eliminate the unwholesome, evil dharmas” — this is called a practitioner. One who is able single-mindedly to believe in and understand emptiness, signlessness, and wishlessness, and who for the sake of the fruits of stream-enterer, once-returner, non-returner, and arhat cuts off the various defilements, is called a practitioner. One who seeks the wholesome dharmas and constantly goes about asking questions is called a practitioner. One who is able to give rise to the resolve to ferry all beings across is called a practitioner. One who diligently practices the various path-assisting dharmas, acting in the scriptures as they are taught, and one who single-mindedly seeks the Buddha way — Śāriputra, these within the Buddha’s Dharma are called practitioners. What is called an attainerer? One who gains the stream-enterer’s escape from the three evil realms is called an attainerer. The once-returner, non-returner, and arhat, who have cut off the various defilements, have stilled their seeking of the path, have done what was to be done, and are well learned in the three trainings — these are called attainerers. I permit such persons to receive offerings; if such persons receive offerings, that is called well receiving offerings.

Śāriputra, if one eats without seeing one’s own faults in food, without seeing the way out of birth-and-death, then it were better that he cut flesh from his own thigh with his own hand and eat it. Why? Because I permit practitioners and attainerers to receive the offerings of others; I do not permit the rest. Śāriputra, what is called a practitioner? If there is a bhikṣu who has firmly resolved, “In this very life I will cut off the fetters and the driving defilements and enter the nirvāṇa of no remainder; I cultivate the noble path as though my head were afire, and I will also cut off and eliminate the unwholesome, evil dharmas” — this is called a practitioner. One who is able single-mindedly to believe in and understand emptiness, signlessness, and wishlessness, and who for the sake of the fruits of stream-enterer, once-returner, non-returner, and arhat cuts off the various defilements, is called a practitioner. One who seeks the wholesome dharmas and constantly goes about asking questions is called a practitioner. One who is able to give rise to the resolve to ferry all beings across is called a practitioner. One who diligently practices the various path-assisting dharmas, acting in the scriptures as they are taught, and one who single-mindedly seeks the Buddha way — Śāriputra, these within the Buddha’s Dharma are called practitioners. What is called an attainerer? One who gains the stream-enterer’s escape from the three evil realms is called an attainerer. The once-returner, non-returner, and arhat, who have cut off the various defilements, have stilled their seeking of the path, have done what was to be done, and are well learned in the three trainings — these are called attainerers. I permit such persons to receive offerings; if such persons receive offerings, that is called well receiving offerings.

[Fetters and driving defilements]The fetters and the driving defilements. Both are names for the defilements: because the defilements bind the body and mind and form the fruits of suffering, they are called “fetters”; because they cause beings to sink in the sea of birth-and-death, they are also called “driving defilements.” There are nine fetters and ten driving defilements. [Nine fetters]The fetter of craving (greed and love), the fetter of anger (hatred), the fetter of pride (arrogance), the fetter of delusion (ignorance), the fetter of doubt (doubting the true Dharma), the fetter of views (the view of self, extreme views, wrong views, and so on), the fetter of grasping (craving and attaching by false reckoning to views and to precepts), the fetter of avarice (hoarding wealth), and the fetter of envy (resenting others). The ten driving defilements, also called the ten delusions or the ten fundamental afflictions, are: one, greed — craving the five sense pleasures; two, anger — hatred without patience; three, delusion — ignorance and lack of understanding; four, pride — arrogance and self-conceit; five, doubt — skepticism and unbelief; six, the view of self — grasping at the five aggregates as one’s body and mind; seven, extreme views — grasping at the two views of annihilation and eternalism; eight, wrong views — denying cause and effect and destroying all wholesome deeds; nine, the view of taking views — holding to fixed opinions, regarding what is not a fruit as a fruit; ten, the view of the efficacy of precepts — holding to wrong precepts, regarding what is not a cause as a cause. The first five are the five blunt driving defilements; the last five are the five sharp driving defilements. “Driving defilement” is another name for the defilements, because the defilements cause beings to wander in birth-and-death.

[Nirvāṇa of no remainder]When the two delusions of views and of thought, together with the body of the five aggregates one has received, are all extinguished without remainder, that is called the nirvāṇa of no remainder. [Path-assisting dharmas]The thirty-seven articles of the path — such as the four foundations of mindfulness and the four right exertions — that assist calm and insight are called path-assisting dharmas. They also assist the fruit of virtue, and each of the practices assists the others, hence they are called path-assisting dharmas. [Thirty-seven articles of the path]Also called the thirty-seven aids to enlightenment, namely: the four foundations of mindfulness, the four right exertions, the four bases of psychic power, the five faculties, the five powers, the seven factors of enlightenment, and the eightfold noble path — thirty-seven articles in all. Being the important provisions for cultivating the path, they are called the “thirty-seven articles of the path.” [Three trainings]The training in morality, the training in concentration, and the training in wisdom. Morality is the precepts, set forth in the Vinaya; it prevents people from committing all evil deeds of body, speech, and mind. Concentration is meditation, set forth in the sūtras; it enables people to still their deliberations and clarify the mind. Wisdom is insight, set forth in the abhidharma; it enables people to discover the truth and cut off delusion. By cultivating these three trainings one may, through morality, gain concentration; through concentration, give rise to wisdom; and in the end obtain the out-of-defilements fruit of the path. Hence the three trainings are also called the “three uncontaminated trainings.” [Out-of-defilements]“Defilement” is another name for the afflictions, meaning leakage; “out-of-defilements” means being pure and free of afflictions.
